question: The owner: the site lacks the 'so what' - a reader sees CO2, temperature, sea level and ice and cannot connect them to consequences for people. Which primary, redistributable datasets express each measurement's consequence in human terms (coasts, disasters and displacement, heat and health, warming-level futures and children's lifetimes, food and water, fossil-fuel air pollution)? One researcher per domain; an adversarial verifier re-read each producer's terms and data; a critic reviewed coverage.

research.scope: SEA LEVEL -> PEOPLE ON COASTS (how many people live on low-lying coastal land, and how many are exposed to sea-level rise and coastal flooding, by country and for the world)
research.notes:
I checked all the requested sources live on 2026-10-11, without writing anything to disk; files were parsed in memory only.

Best fit for the dashboard:
1. **Kulp & Strauss 2019 supplementary CSVs (CC BY 4.0, open download, World and 135 countries).** These give the clearest "so what" for the sea-level number: people on land below the future high-tide line, and below the annual flood line, today and in 2050 and 2100 under each RCP.
2. **OECD coastal flooding exposure.** Open, attribution-only data terms. The SDMX API works for scripts and gives the World and about 230 countries every year from 2000 to 2022, as the share of people inside the 1-in-100-year coastal floodplain. The flood hazard is fixed, so trends reflect population, not rising seas.
3. **Lancet 2.3.3 (people less than 1 m above the sea).** Already researched and the Lancet source is already registered, so adding this workbook as an artifact is the least work. Note that the 2026 report (28 Oct) will probably replace the file.
4. **LECZ v3 (CC BY 4.0).** This is the authoritative "people within 5 m / 10 m of sea level, urban vs rural" series for 1990, 2000 and 2015. NASA Earthdata now needs a free login for the actual GET (HEAD misleadingly returns 200), so it is a manual download. The World Bank WDI republishes the core shares (EN.POP.EL5M.*) under CC BY 4.0 through an open API, but WDI is a copy with stale methodology text, so use it only as a cross-check twin.
5. **Kirezci/Young 2024 figshare (CC BY 4.0).** Adds "people flooded by the sea in an average year" by country, with RCP and SSP futures. The national table was read through HTTP Range requests from a 602 MB zip; the paper itself (MDPI) is blocked to scripts.

Display-only and world-only:
- The IPCC AR6 WGII SPM statements B.4.5 ("exposed population doubles at 0.75 m, triples at 1.4 m") and D.3.3 ("896 million in the LECZ in 2020, beyond 1 billion by 2050") fit the existing display-only IPCC pattern. The IPCC copyright page was re-read today and is unchanged.
- Reimann et al. 2023 (Cambridge Prisms, CC BY) gives world totals only. The Reimann 2023 Nature Communications paper covers the Mediterranean only, so it is not usable here.

Rejected:
- Climate Central's own coastal tools: non-commercial only, no bulk or automated download, no distribution of meaning-changing modifications, and no data file. Add to the Rejected list.

Method warnings for the owner:
- The choice of elevation model changes the answer by about 3 times. For Bangladesh, MERIT-based LECZ and WDI give 8% of people below 5 m, while CoastalDEM gives 28 M below the annual flood line today. Every view should name its elevation model.
- All of these are bathtub-style exposure estimates that ignore sea walls, so they should be labelled "live on land at risk", not "will be flooded".
- Kulp & Strauss has an Author Correction (2019) that changed some numbers in the text; check the CSVs against the corrected text before quoting text numbers.

Terms pages blocked to scripts:
- oecd.org (403): terms read from the Internet Archive snapshot of 2026-10-10.
- mdpi.com (403).
- nature.com (cookie redirect): licences read from Europe PMC and Crossref instead.

candidates.name: Kulp & Strauss 2019, 'New elevation data triple estimates of global vulnerability to sea-level rise and coastal flooding' (Nature Communications 10:4844), Supplementary Data 1-4 CSVs

candidates.licence_quote: Open Access This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, which permits use, sharing, adaptation, distribution and reproduction in any medium or format, as long as you give appropriate credit to the original author(s) and the source, provide a link to the Creative Commons license, and indicate if changes were made.
candidates.measures: How many people (in millions, plus a percentage version) live on land below the local high-tide line ('Perm') and below the local once-a-year coastal flood level ('RL1'). Given for today's sea level and for 2050 and 2100 under RCP2.6, RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, using two sea-level projection sets (K14, K17) with 5th/50th/95th percentiles, and four elevation models (CoastalDEM, SRTM, JAXA, MERIT). Covers the World, small island developing states and 135 countries. Supplementary Data 2 gives people living 0 to 10 m above local high tide, in 1 m steps, by country (CoastalDEM).
candidates.plain_phrase: people whose homes are on land that rising seas will put below the high-tide line, or under a flood every year
candidates.geography: World, small island developing states (SIDS) and 135 countries; Supplementary Data 2 and 3 cover about 160 countries
candidates.years: Population fixed at LandScan 2010. Sea levels for today, 2050 and 2100
candidates.access: open download (Springer static content; all files returned HTTP 200 to curl on 2026-10-11). nature.com article pages redirect scripts to a cookie login, so the licence text was read from the Europe PMC full text (PMC6820795) and Crossref (vor licence CC BY 4.0)
candidates.data_url: https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-019-12808-z/MediaObjects/41467_2019_12808_MOESM4_ESM.csv (Supplementary Data 1, millions, 253,535 bytes). Also MOESM5_ESM.csv (Supplementary Data 2, 0-10 m bands, CoastalDEM, 12,572 bytes), MOESM7_ESM.csv (Supplementary Data 4, percent of population, 353,145 bytes) and MOESM3_ESM.pdf (descriptions of the files)
candidates.already_researched: no (the CoastalDEM method is mentioned only as the basis of Lancet 2.3.3 in docs/research/sources-impacts.json)
candidates.caveats: Verified values: World 'Present day' CoastalDEM median is 110 M below high tide and 250 M below the annual flood level (SRTM: 28 M and 65 M). Bangladesh: 9.3 M and 28 M. Population is held at its 2010 distribution (LandScan 2010), so the future columns show where today's people live relative to future seas; they are not projections of future population. Sea-level inputs are pre-AR6 (Kopp 2014 and Kopp 2017), so label them as projections. The method is a bathtub model that ignores sea walls, so the Netherlands and other protected coasts are overstated; this is exposure, not flooding. An Author Correction (doi:10.1038/s41467-019-13552-0, 12 Dec 2019) changed several numbers in the text (for example 230 M, not 250 M, below 1 m). Check the CSVs against the corrected text before quoting text numbers. Country names are plain text, not ISO codes, and need a crosswalk. The data availability statement says the CoastalDEM grid itself is non-commercial research only, but the national exposure tables are part of the CC BY article. Countries with maximum exposure under 0.01 M were dropped.

candidates.caveats: The headline from ESSD: between 750 million and nearly 1.1 billion people lived in the 10 m zone in 2015, with nearly 300 million in the higher-risk 5 m zone (core inputs). The ESSD paper is CC BY 4.0. The old sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu host is retired; use the DOI 10.7927/d1x1-d702 and the ESDIS record. The data are .xlsm (macro-enabled Excel): parse them as data and never run the macros. The latest year is 2015. Living in the zone is a measure of exposure, not harm. Open shortcut: the World Bank WDI republishes the core LECZ v3 shares as EN.POP.EL5M.ZS, EN.POP.EL5M.UR.ZS and EN.POP.EL5M.RU.ZS (License_Type 'CC BY-4.0'; Source names LECZ v3, doi:10.7927/d1x1-d702). They come from the open API (World 2015 = 4.06%, consistent with about 300 M below 5 m; Netherlands 53.7%, Viet Nam 29.7%, Bangladesh 8.4%). WDI is a copy, though, and its methodology text still describes GRUMPv1 (v2). Under rule 2 it can only be a convenience twin or a cross-check of the producer's file. The low MERIT-based Bangladesh share differs sharply from CoastalDEM-based figures, so the choice of elevation model must be stated.

candidates.caveats: Verified values: World 2.32% of people in the 1-in-100-year coastal floodplain in 2020 (2.36% in 2000); Netherlands 59.2%; Bangladesh 0.88%. Only shares are published. A head count needs a population series (a calculated value, to be labelled as such). The hazard is a fixed present-day map (Muis et al. 2016 global coastal flood hazard, doi:10.1038/ncomms11969), so year-to-year change reflects where people live, not rising seas. It ignores flood defences, so the Netherlands is overstated. The low Bangladesh value shows hazard-map limits in deltas. The terms carry a third-party clause: the inputs are the Muis et al. hazard maps (CC BY article), the GHSL population grid (JRC, CC BY 4.0) and ESA CCI land cover. The SDMX key has 12 dimensions; the DSD 2.1 structure adds a LIVESTOCK dimension, so pin version 2.0.

research.scope: DISASTERS -> HOMES AND LIVES (people displaced, killed or affected by weather and climate disasters, world and country, over time)
research.notes:
I read docs/sources.md (registry and Rejected list), docs/research/sources-impacts.json (IDMC, EM-DAT, NOAA, OWID and Climate Central entries, plus verifier verdicts) and pipeline/sources/idmc-gidd.yaml first. Everything below was re-checked on 2026-10-11.

The main finding: no openly licensed global time series of disaster DEATHS exists. Every multi-hazard mortality series traces back to EM-DAT: OWID, WDI EN.CLC.MDAT.ZS (WB labels it CC BY 4.0, but its source is EM-DAT, so EM-DAT's terms apply), the WMO Atlas, IFRC Montandon and probably WHO GHE. EM-DAT's terms (no substantial part, no derivative databases) and the CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 FAIR archive (v2, 2026-04-30) were re-confirmed, so the rejection stands. Heat deaths are already covered by Lancet Countdown. The real 'homes and lives' backbone is IDMC GIDD. It is already registered, but the domain needs it exported.

IDMC details (checked 2026-10-11):
(1) The licence in the API OpenAPI document is unchanged: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO, with 'Derived Works: Must be shared under the same license terms.'
(2) The country-year displacement-export has only a disaster TOTAL plus Disaster Stock; the hazard split lives in the event file. disaster-export has Hazard Category, Type and Sub-Type per event (CRED classification), and both exports accept hazard_type__in.
(3) GRID 2026 publishes the 2025 split: storms 17.9M, floods under 7.9M, wildfires over 694,000, geophysical about 2.5M, out of 29.9M. 13.6M people were living in disaster displacement at the end of 2025.
(4) The idmc-gidd yaml's 'The GIDD web page has no button for this export' looks outdated. In the website bundle (release-website-components.idmcdb.org/js/main.bundle.js?bundle=3), the GIDD download panel's 'Annual displacement data' > 'Excel' link switches to gidd/disasters/disaster-export/ when the cause filter is 'disaster'. The country-profile widget also offers 'Disaster events aggregated data (.xlsx)'. A person should confirm this in a browser and could then record the event file by hand now.
(5) The API still returns 403 without client_id. IDMC's IDU (last 180 days, same licence) could supply a 'this year so far' figure later.

New, strong and open: World Bank Global Findex 2025 (CC BY 4.0, open API, about 98 low- and middle-income countries, 2024). It is measured survey data on the share of adults hit by a disaster or severe weather in the past three years, the share who lost income, and the share whose home or livestock was damaged. It is the most direct layperson 'so what' found, but it is a single wave with no high-income countries. Rentschler et al. 2022 (CC BY 4.0, 188 countries, 1.81 billion people exposed to 1-in-100-year floods) is a good modelled exposure snapshot; transcribe it from Supplementary Table 1.

Weaker:
- Global Flood Database: CC BY-NC 4.0 per the producer README, but it stops in 2018 and its DFO columns must not be used.
- Groundswell: projected. The PDF says non-commercial only, which conflicts with the repository's CC BY 3.0 IGO tag, so use the stricter statement.

Unusable:
- IFRC GO/Montandon: EM-DAT-style prohibitions.
- UNDRR Sendai Monitor, undrr.org and PreventionWeb: Cloudflare 403, so the terms could not be read. The UN SDG route is already rejected.
- DesInventar: no data licence; sub-national records; being replaced by DELTA Resilience.
- Dartmouth Flood Observatory: scholarly and education use only, and the host refused connections.
- WHO GHE 'Natural disasters': the WHO data terms forbid alteration beyond styling, and the cause mixes in earthquakes.

NOAA billion-dollar: US-only and retired in May 2025. The CSV still returns HTTP 200 and is public domain. Its continuation by Climate Central is non-commercial with no bulk download.

Not checked: the World Bank DDH catalogue entry for Rentschler's rasters (API rate-limited), and the exact depth thresholds in Rentschler's Methods.

candidates.name: IDMC GIDD disaster event export: internal displacements by hazard type (flood, storm, wildfire, drought, extreme temperature, wet mass movement), by country and year, 2008-2025
candidates.producer: Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC), Norwegian Refugee Council
candidates.licence_quote: Data is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-Non-Commercial-Share Alike 3.0 IGO license.

research.scope: What each bit of warming means, and for whom (children, generations, warming levels)
research.notes:
The strongest new pairing for the temperature chart is Grant et al. 2025 (CC BY 4.0). Its SI PDF has 18 country-by-birth-cohort tables (1960-2020, every 10 years) for six hazards at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 C. Each cell gives absolute people in thousands and the percent of the cohort. World headlines (52% / 62 million of 2020 births at 1.5 C vs 92% / 111 million at 3.5 C; 16% / 13 million of 1960 births) come from the main text, Results section; the SI tables have no world row. The SI PDF is at static-content.springer.com, opens without login, and is extractable with pdftotext -layout, though country names wrap. The Zenodo deposit (10.5281/zenodo.15097896, cc-by-4.0) holds only heatwave inputs for a rerun, not the results.

The second strongest is the IIASA Climate Solutions Explorer v1.1 on Zenodo (CC BY 4.0, CSV). It is the only open, machine-readable source found with population exposure by warming level (1.2-3.5 C) for countries and the World, plus 'avoided by 1.5 C' tables. Its exposure measure is a composite hazard score defined by the authors, so the threshold coded in each variable string must be decoded and explained before any number is published.

wb-cckp is already registered. Further people-relevant CMIP6 indicators answer on the same API with the same licence: heat-index days, tropical nights above 26/29 C, and days above 40 C. They are grouped by SSP and period, not by warming level, and are averaged over land area rather than population.

IPCC WGII SPM.3 data is not on CEDA: data.ceda.ac.uk/badc lists only ar6_wg1, ar6_sr15, ipcc-ddc and ipcc-ddc-regions, and the CEDA catalogue returns no WGII titles. It is held by the IPCC DDC at Columbia/SEDAC as the AR6 Risk Assessment Database (doi:10.7927/pzv8-ta24). The DDC host is behind Cloudflare and SEDAC timed out on 2026-10-11, so the file needs a manual download. Its licence conflicts: CC BY 4.0 inside the file versus CC BY-SA 4.0 in DataCite. IPCC's own figure terms forbid altering figures, so redraw from the data. WGII SPM.4 is not a risk-by-warming-level figure, and no data for it was found.

Thiery 2021 is AAAS-copyright and science.org blocks scripts; its open successor is Grant 2025. Lange 2020's paper is CC BY, and its derived ISIMIP2b exposure grids are CC0 (doi:10.48364/ISIMIP.924045), but they are heavy and the paper has no numeric warming-level table. Climate Impact Explorer was re-checked: the methodology PDF of 5 Nov 2025 still has only a usage-with-citation sentence and no licence. UNICEF's child heatwave report has country annex tables, but UNICEF's terms require prior written permission, so it is effectively excluded.

Not checked: the Save the Children 'Born into the Climate Crisis' reports (secondary, built on Thiery/Grant) and the IPCC AR6 WGI Atlas (already researched, CC BY, IPCC regions rather than countries). The Lancet Countdown 2026 report (launches 28 Oct 2026) should be re-checked afterwards for child- and age-specific heat indicators. All checks were made on 2026-10-11 with read-only curl, WebFetch and in-memory parsing; no files were written.

candidates.name: Grant et al. 2025, Nature 641:374-379, 'Global emergence of unprecedented lifetime exposure to climate extremes': Supplementary Tables 1-18 (people per birth cohort facing unprecedented lifetime exposure, by country, at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 C)
candidates.producer: Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB-HYDR, Grant, Thiery et al.) with ISIMIP modellers; published by Springer Nature (Nature)
candidates.licence_quote: Open Access This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, which permits use, sharing, adaptation, distribution and reproduction in any medium or format, as long as you give appropriate credit to the original author(s) and the source, provide a link to the Creative Commons licence, and indicate if changes were made.
candidates.measures: For each country and each birth cohort (1960, 1970, ... 2020): how many people (thousands) and what share of the cohort will live through a lifetime total of heatwaves, river floods, droughts, crop failures, wildfires or tropical cyclones that would be virtually impossible (beyond the 99.99th percentile) in a pre-industrial climate. There are 18 tables: six hazards times three warming pathways (1.5, 2.5, 3.5 C by 2100). The main text gives world headlines: for heatwaves, 52% of people born in 2020 (62 million) under 1.5 C versus 92% (111 million) under 3.5 C, against about 16% (13 million) of people born in 1960 whatever the scenario. Under 3.5 C, 29% of the 2020 cohort faces unprecedented crop failures and 14% unprecedented river floods. Under 1.5 C, 104 countries have most of the 2020 cohort facing unprecedented heatwaves; under 3.5 C, 167 do.
candidates.plain_phrase: children born today who will live through more heatwaves than anyone could have in a world without climate change, compared with their grandparents
candidates.geography: Country (about 180 countries, e.g. Table 1 has India, Nigeria, United Kingdom, Brazil). The SI tables have no world row; world figures come from the main text only (a sum of country rows would be the site's own computation).
candidates.years: Birth cohorts 1960-2020 (tables every 10 years), lifetime exposure along warming pathways to 2100; published 7 May 2025 (SI PDF last-modified 28 Apr 2025)
candidates.access: paper table transcription. The SI PDF is open with no login (HTTP 200) and pdftotext -layout extracts the tables, but long country names wrap over 2-4 lines. A heatwave-only rerun input is on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.15097896 (data.zip, 225.6 MB, licence cc-by-4.0). The code is at github.com/VUB-HYDR/2025_Grant_etal_Nature: its README says MIT, but the GitHub API reports no licence file.
candidates.caveats: Modelled from ISIMIP2b impact models: CMIP5-era, 4 GCMs, ensembles shrinking at high warming for crop failure, drought, flood and cyclone. 'Unprecedented' is a statistical definition (more than the 99.99th percentile of pre-industrial lifetime exposure), not a count of deaths. The 2.7 C current-policies case appears only in SI figures, not in the tables. Some small island states show 0 (0) for recent cohorts. The SI PDF has no licence line of its own; the article's CC BY 4.0 statement sits directly under the SI link on the article page, so cite the table number and page. The cyclone fraction nearly doubles when restricted to exposed regions (6% to 11% at 1.5 C). Lifetime figures assume fixed life expectancy and ignore migration. This is the CC BY successor to Thiery et al. 2021 (Science), which is AAAS-copyright.

candidates.name: Climate Solutions Explorer: hazard, impacts and exposure data v1.1 (IIASA; Werning et al. 2024)
candidates.producer: International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), with KAIST
candidates.licence_quote: License CC BY 4.0 ... When using this data for any analysis, figures or tables, please clearly state the release version v1.1 (README.txt in the Zenodo record; Zenodo metadata licence id cc-by-4.0)
candidates.measures: Country and world tables of how many people (on SSP1-5 population projections) and how much land are exposed to at least low, medium or high hazard from about 42 indicators at global warming levels of 1.2, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 and 3.5 C. Indicators include heatwave days from wet-bulb heat-stress events, tropical nights above 20 C, water stress, drought intensity, heavy-rain days and cooling degree days. There are also 'avoided impacts' tables: the people and land spared by holding warming to 1.5 C rather than 2, 2.5, 3 or 3.5 C. FINDINGS AND GAPS: (1) The strongest open 'so what' for food is the GRFC 2026 weather-extremes-driver series (CC BY 4.0, 87.5 million people in 2025, 96.6 million in 2024). Pair it with FAOSTAT FS for the scale of hunger (644.6 million undernourished in 2025). FAOSTAT is already registered; only the FS artifact is new. No primary, open dataset attributes a share of hunger to climate change. The closest is Lancet Countdown 1.4.1 ('123.7 million more people' food insecure in 2023, associated with more heatwave days and drought months), but its values are NOT downloadable: the 1.4 link serves only the 1.4.2 marine workbook. Re-check after the Lancet Countdown 2026 launch on 28 Oct 2026. (2) Crop yields and warming: Ortiz-Bobea 2021 is a subscription article. Its CISER replication data has custom terms behind an AWS WAF CAPTCHA (not bypassed; needs a human), but arXiv 2007.10415v2 is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Its figures differ from the published version (9 vs 7 years; 30-33% vs 26-34%). Hultgren 2025 (article CC BY-NC-ND), ISIMIP3b (CC0) and SPEIbase (ODbL) are already in docs/research/sources-impacts.json and were not repeated. Jagermeyr et al. 2021 Nature Food (doi:10.1038/s43016-021-00400-y) has no open licence on Crossref (TDM only); its numbers derive from ISIMIP3b, already researched. (3) Water: Aqueduct 4.0 country rankings are CC BY 4.0 per WRI's GitHub data dictionary and Open Data Commitment, but carry no population. 'People in extremely water-stressed countries' needs a join with un-wpp-2024. WRI's '4 billion people at least one month' needs gridded sub-basin data plus a population grid, so it is out of scope. (4) Glaciers as water supply: Immerzeel 2020 (article subscription; Zenodo data CC BY 4.0, basin units only). Also checked: Viviroli et al. 2020 Nature Sustainability (subscription; Dryad typology only; the authors say the rising dependence is 'mainly due to increased local water consumption' and runoff changes 'play only a minor role', so weak for warming) and Pritchard 2019 Nature (subscription, TDM-only licence). No open country table of people depending on glacier melt was found. (5) Drought exposure: Lancet 1.2.2 (registered entry; workbook not yet an artifact; land area, not people) and the UNCCD dashboard (CC BY-NC 2.0, partial self-reported coverage). IDMC drought displacement is already registered (idmc-gidd). NOT FULLY CHECKED: UNICEF water vulnerability (data.unicef.org terms returned 403; the 2021 snapshot is not climate-attributed). SOFI 2025/2026 report licences (the FAO OKR copyright page returned 403; only FAOSTAT database terms apply to FS values). The fsinplatform.org GRFC data files return 403 to scripts and need a manual download. The FAOSTAT FS domain metadata (fenixservices API) returned non-JSON today, so third-party rows (JME stunting, JMP water) need their terms confirmed before publication.

research.scope: Burning fossil fuels and clean power -> health: deaths from air pollution caused by burning coal, oil and gas (world, by country, by sector and fuel)
research.notes:
Three usable fossil-fuel estimates, all verified against the files themselves:
(1) Lancet Countdown 2025 indicator 3.2.1, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Best world time series, 2007-2022, by sector and fuel. Fossil-fuel deaths were 2.52 million in 2022. No country values in this vintage.
(2) Lelieveld et al. 2023: the EDMOND deposit doi:10.17617/3.T7XAXH is CC0, even though the BMJ article is CC BY-NC. It gives 200 countries for 2019, plus phase-out scenarios. Ref minus noFF reproduces the paper's 5.13 million exactly. Best for a country map and for 'lives saved if fossil fuels are phased out'.
(3) McDuffie et al. 2021: the supplements are CC BY 4.0. Countries for 2017, with shares by fuel and sector. Reproduces 1.05 million. A good cross-check, and it has a 'coal power' share.

The estimates span roughly 1 to 5 million deaths a year, depending on the risk function and on whether ozone and all-cause mortality are included. Per docs/sources.md rule 4, show them as twins with an explainer, never blended. Suggested pairing for the clean-power row: Lancet 3.2.1 'deaths from coal burned in power plants' (610,189 in 2022) next to the clean share of electricity, and the Lelieveld country 'avoidable deaths' map for drill-down.

The other four go under Rejected or the restricted classes:
- WHO GHO AIR_41: WHO's own dataset terms are bespoke ('public health purposes', no alteration without written authorisation). The CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO label comes only from a World Bank Data360 aggregator record. Not fossil-specific.
- IHME GBD: click-through contract that forbids derivative works and third-party downloads, with the credit line 'All rights reserved'. Not fossil-specific.
- State of Global Air: 'distribution without alteration', built on GBD values.
- Vohra 2021: '© 2021 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved'.

Timing: the Lancet Countdown 2026 report launches on 28 Oct 2026, in 17 days. Indicator 3.2.1 will probably be reissued under a new file name, possibly with a later final year and perhaps country values. It may be worth waiting before building the artifact, or building it with a discover rule.

Access notes: EDMOND's HTML landing page sits behind an Anubis proof-of-work challenge for scripts, but its official Dataverse API (dataset JSON and /api/access/datafile/<id>) served everything directly, which is not a workaround. nature.com and ScienceDirect block scripts; licences were read from Europe PMC full text and Crossref.

Not pursued: Henneman et al. 2023 (Science, US coal power deaths) is US-only, and its Europe PMC full text returned HTTP 500. The EEA air-quality health risk assessment is CC BY 4.0 per the EEA catalogue, but it covers Europe only and is not fossil-specific; its files sit in a Nextcloud share that was not fully parsed.

Nothing was written to disk; all files were read in memory by piping curl into Python.

The article itself (BMJ 2023;383:e077784) says: 'This is an Open Access article distributed in accordance with the Creative Commons Attribution Non Commercial (CC BY-NC 4.0) license, which permits others to distribute, remix, adapt, build upon this work non-commercially, and license their derivative works on different terms, provided the original work is properly cited and the use is non-commercial.'
candidates.measures: Excess deaths from outdoor PM2.5 plus ozone in 2019, for 200 countries, 27 GBD regions and the world. Each file holds one scenario: the reference case, no fossil fuels, half of fossil fuels removed, a quarter removed, and no human-made emissions. All-cause and cause-specific columns (IHD, stroke, COPD, lung cancer, diabetes, child and adult LRI, ozone COPD) each come with 95% CI columns. Fossil-attributable deaths = ref minus noFF. Checked for the WORLD row on the all-cause column 'NCD+LRI+LRI5-+CPO3': 8,341,770 minus 3,215,143 = 5,126,627, which matches the paper's 5.13 million. Examples computed the same way: India about 1.35 million, China about 1.82 million, the United States about 84,000.
candidates.plain_phrase: lives that could be saved each year in each country if coal, oil and gas were no longer burned
candidates.geography: World, 27 GBD regions and 200 countries. Countries are named, with no ISO codes.
candidates.access: open download through the official Dataverse API: files came back as real xlsx (PK header). The EDMOND HTML landing page puts scripts behind an Anubis bot challenge, so a person should look at the human-readable licence badge once. The API worked without any workaround.
candidates.caveats: The highest of the three estimates. It uses the FUSION risk model, all-cause mortality and includes ozone; the paper quotes 8.34 million deaths from all outdoor air pollution, against 4.45 million in GBD 2019. Getting fossil-fuel deaths means subtracting two scenario files. That is allowed under CC0, but it must be labelled as calculated by us, and CIs cannot be subtracted, so quote the paper's CI for the world. The model gives almost no deaths left in high-income countries without fossil fuels (Germany 0, UK 108), so nearly all their air-pollution deaths count as fossil. That is a property of the model and needs an explainer. Country names carry trailing tab characters and need mapping to ISO3 (US is 'United States of America'). There is only one year, so it cannot be a time series. The repo has 1.27 GB code.tar.gz, which is not needed.

Fetched MOESM4 to stdout: 1,769 rows, header Place,Total,SeaLevel,CoastalDEM_Perm_p5..., World 'Present day' row CoastalDEM_Perm_p50=110, CoastalDEM_RL1_p50=250, SRTM 28/65. verdicts.evidence: The licence block in the article XML is CC BY 4.0 and includes 'The images or other third party material in this article are included in the article's Creative Commons license, unless indicated otherwise'. The Data availability statement says 'All exposure analyses (national populations on vulnerable land) that support the findings of our study are available within this article and its supplementary information files', and the CoastalDEM grid itself is 'available at no cost from Climate Central for non-commercial research use'. The non-commercial restriction applies to the elevation grid, not to the published national tables. The ESM CSVs carry no separate licence, so they fall under the article licence (Springer Nature practice; no contrary notice found). The authors are the producers, so this is a primary source. The Author Correction confirms a code error that was fixed during review but left out of the text: abstract '230 M' (not 250 M) below 1 m; China 18-32%; '7-20 million' (not 10-25 M) on surge-threatened land, and others. Quote CSV values, not text numbers, and check that they agree. Caveats in the proposal (LandScan 2010 population held fixed, pre-AR6 K14/K17 sea levels, bathtub model ignoring defences, country names in plain text) are consistent with what was seen. Not registered in pipeline/sources; not in the Rejected list.

Licence: the CC BY 4.0 sentence is quoted verbatim from the article's 'Rights and permissions' section on nature.com. It sits directly after the 'Supplementary Information (download PDF)' link. The SI PDF has no licence line of its own: its cover says 'In the format provided by the authors and unedited', and a scan of all 115 pages found no licence, copyright or Creative Commons text. critic:
Coverage critique of the "so what" consequence datasets, checked on 2026-10-11. Everything below was checked by me; licence text is quoted from the producer unless marked otherwise.

## 1. Measurements still lacking a strong, usable consequence dataset

**CO2 in the air (ppm): gap.** None of the six domains paired anything with the concentration itself. The best fixes are in section 2: Medek 2017 and Weyant 2018, which link higher CO2 directly to less nutritious food.

**Arctic September sea ice: gap.** Nothing was paired with it. Any human pairing for sea ice is honestly weak and mostly Arctic-local. The defensible bridge is Rantanen 2022 (the Arctic warming about 4x faster) plus Ramage 2021 or Hjort 2018 (people on thawing permafrost).
- Notz & Stroeve 2016 (about 3 m² of September ice lost per tonne of CO2) is in Science and not open access. Treat it as display-only.

**Fossil CO2 emissions: partly covered.** Lancet 3.2.1, Lelieveld and McDuffie are deaths from the air pollution that comes with burning fossil fuels, not harm from the CO2 itself. Two direct emissions-to-people links are missing:
- **An already-accepted source was under-used.** Lenton 2023 (CC BY 4.0) was paired only with temperature, but its abstract also says: "The lifetime emissions of ~3.5 global average citizens today (or ~1.2 average US citizens) expose one future person to unprecedented heat by end-of-century." It should also pair with emissions.
- Bressler 2021 (section 2) gives deaths per tonne of CO2.

**Global warming: well covered.** Lenton 2023, Grant 2025, Lancet heat deaths, Lancet 1.1.4 sleep loss, and the CCKP heat days.

**Sea level: covered.** Kulp & Strauss 2019 (Crossref CC BY 4.0 confirmed) and LECZ v3. None of them is a time series of people affected; they are scenarios or one-year snapshots.

**Clean share of electricity: adequate.**
- Lelieveld's own EDMOND files include a no-fossil-fuel scenario (mortality_countries_2019_noFF.xlsx), which gives deaths avoided by clean power.
- A positive "work" pairing is missing. IRENA/ILO renewable energy jobs is in section 2.

**Cross-cutting gaps:**
- There is no open source for disaster deaths (EM-DAT is no-derivatives, WHO GHE no-derivatives, Sendai unclear).
- There is no open poverty consequence. Jafino 2020 (section 2) fills it.

## 2. Important open datasets nobody checked (licences checked by me)

**a) Bressler 2021, "The mortality cost of carbon", Nature Communications 12:4467** (doi:10.1038/s41467-021-24487-w). Pairs with emissions. Score 4.
- Licence: CC BY 4.0. Crossref lists it for the version of record; nature.com says "Open Access This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License".
- Values, transcribed from the text:
  - 2.26×10⁻⁴ excess deaths per tonne of CO2 emitted in 2020, so "adding 4,434 metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2020 … causes one excess death globally" between 2020 and 2100.
  - 83 million cumulative excess deaths by 2100 in the baseline (about 4.1 °C), against 9 million on a 2.4 °C path.
- Caveats: it is modelled with a single model (DICE-EMR), and the low-to-high range runs from −1.71×10⁻⁴ to 6.78×10⁻⁴, so it crosses zero. Label it modelled and always show the range.
- Not in the repo (grep found nothing).

**b) Medek, Schwartz & Myers 2017, Environmental Health Perspectives 125:087002** (doi:10.1289/EHP41). Pairs with CO2 in the air. Score 4.
- Licence: public domain. The PMC XML says "All content is public domain unless otherwise noted."
- Abstract: "By 2050 … an additional 1.6% or 148.4 million of the world's population may be placed at risk of protein deficiency because of eCO2", including 53 million in India.
- Country-specific results are stated, but I did not open the 121 KB supplement to confirm a full country table.
- Modelled, at roughly 550 ppm with today's diets.

**c) Weyant et al. 2018, PLOS Medicine 15(7):e1002586** (doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.1002586). Pairs with CO2 in the air. Score 4.
- Licence: "an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited."
- Finding: CO2-driven loss of zinc and iron in crops adds about 125.8 million DALYs from 2015 to 2050 (95% interval 113.6–138.9 million).
- Scenario: about 400 ppm rising to 550 ppm by 2050, against about 480 ppm on a Paris-consistent path.
- 137 countries. Country results are described as S4 and S9 Tables; I did not open those files.

**d) Ramage et al. 2021, "Population living on permafrost in the Arctic", Population and Environment** (doi:10.1007/s11111-020-00370-6). Pairs with Arctic sea ice. Score 3.
- Licence: CC BY 4.0. The Springer page says "This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License."
- Values: 4,942,685 people in 1,162 permafrost settlements (2017); 3.3 million in settlements where permafrost is projected to thaw by 2050 (RCP4.5).
- Table 6 is by region within countries, which is sub-national and breaks the rule. Use only the pan-Arctic total, and get the owner's ruling on whether a multi-country total is allowed.

**e) Hjort et al. 2018, Nature Communications 9:5147** (doi:10.1038/s41467-018-07557-4). Pairs with Arctic sea ice. Score 3.
- Licence: CC BY 4.0, from Crossref only (version of record).
- Abstract: "nearly four million people and 70% of current infrastructure in the permafrost domain are in areas with high potential for thaw" by 2050.
- Bridge source: Rantanen et al. 2022, Communications Earth & Environment (doi:10.1038/s43247-022-00498-3), Crossref CC BY 4.0, for the Arctic warming nearly four times faster than the globe.

**f) Jafino, Walsh, Rozenberg & Hallegatte 2020, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9417** (hdl:10986/34555). Cross-cutting (poverty). Score 4.
- Licence: the World Bank repository record says dc.rights "CC BY 3.0 IGO", rights URI http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/igo.
- Value: 32 to 132 million people pushed into extreme poverty by climate change by 2030 in most scenarios.
- World and region only; modelled.

**g) ILO 2024, "Ensuring safety and health at work in a changing climate"** (ISBN 9789220405079). Cross-cutting (work and deaths). Score 4.
- Licence, from the PDF: "This is an open access work distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License". Also: "This CC license does not apply to non-ILO copyright materials included in this publication."
- Values I confirmed: the licence and a headline of at least 2.41 billion workers exposed to excessive heat (2020).
- Values reported in search results that still need checking against the PDF: 18,970 work deaths a year from excessive heat, 22.85 million injuries, and 26.2 million people with heat-linked kidney disease.
- These complement the published Lancet work-hours indicator.

**h) IRENA and ILO, Renewable energy and jobs: Annual review.** Pairs with clean power. Score 3.
- Licence, from the 2024 edition PDF: "material in this publication may be freely used, shared, copied, reproduced, printed and/or stored, provided that appropriate acknowledgement is given of IRENA as the source and copyright holder", with third-party material excepted. That is attribution-only.
- The 2025 edition (16.6 million jobs in 2024, published January 2026) is reported in search results, but the URL forms I guessed returned redirects. A person may need to fetch it by hand.

**i) Callahan & Mankin 2022, Climatic Change 172:40** (doi:10.1007/s10584-022-03387-y). Pairs with emissions (country-by-country damages). Score 2.
- Licence: Crossref says CC BY 4.0.
- The country data portal (rcweb.dartmouth.edu/CMIG/national_attribution_2022/prod/) has no licence I could verify.
- Damages are GDP in dollars, not people, and the method is contested. Crossref also shows a correction notice.

## 3. Well-known sources checked and found unusable

**UNDP / Climate Impact Lab Human Climate Horizons** (country deaths projected from warming): excluded.
- The site's "Terms Of Use" link goes to undp.org/copyright-terms-use. The live page returns 403, so I read the Internet Archive copy.
- It allows materials only "for the User's personal, non-commercial use, without any right to resell or redistribute them or to compile or create derivative works therefrom".

**WHO 2014, "Quantitative risk assessment of the effects of climate change on selected causes of death"** (the famous "250,000 extra deaths a year"): display-only.
- The PDF says "All rights reserved", and "Requests for permission to reproduce … whether for sale or for non-commercial distribution" go to WHO Press.
- The WHO repository record has no CC rights.

**Kotz et al. 2024** has been retracted (2025-12-03). This is already flagged in sources-impacts.json.

## 4. Candidates wrongly accepted or misclassified

1. **Groundswell Part 2 is misclassified.** The World Bank repository record (hdl:10986/36248) says "CC BY 3.0 IGO", so it is open, not noncommercial. This error is in the safe direction.
2. **Lelieveld 2023 is open only through the data deposit.** The BMJ article itself is CC BY-NC 4.0 (Crossref). The EDMOND deposit (doi:10.17617/3.T7XAXH) is CC0 1.0. Provenance must point at the EDMOND files (mortality_countries_2019_ref.xlsx, _noFF.xlsx and the others), never the article. It covers a single year (2019), not a time series.
3. **FAOSTAT food insecurity and WRI Aqueduct are mis-paired.** Their licences are fine, but they measure baseline hunger and water stress, not consequences attributed to climate. Present them as context, not as what warming does to people.
4. **GRFC 2026's "weather extremes primary driver" is not attribution to climate change.** It includes El Niño and natural variability. The licence is CC BY 4.0 according to reproductions of the rights page; I could not read it on an FAO or FSIN page. Label it "weather extremes", never "caused by warming".
5. **Lancet 2.3.3 should not be the lead sea-level pairing.** It is one cross-section of people below 1 m of future sea-level rise (a simple flooding model), set against an observed series in millimetres. Lead with Kulp & Strauss.
6. **Ortiz-Bobea from the arXiv preprint is weak.** The peer-reviewed version (Nature Climate Change 2021) is paywalled, and the preprint's values may differ from it. Drop it or cite only after checking the two match.
7. **The IPCC AR6 Risk Assessment Database and ISIMIP2b fractions are low value for a lay reader.** One is risk levels and the other is raw exposure fractions that need heavy processing. They are fine as background, not as the headline "so what".
